chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, and Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn Mahiyar, from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, who said:
One of our friends wrote to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): 'With me is a woman I know. Her husband did something and fled from the country. Some of the wife's family followed the husband and said,

key_terms.إِمَّا رَدَدْتُكَ: Or I returned you (to the marriage)
key_terms.فَمَا تَرَى: So what do you see (what is your view)
key_terms.مَضَى الرَّجُلُ عَلَى وَجْهِهِ: The man went upon his direction/continued

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for a woman whose husband fled and was divorced by his family?
ai.summary: This narration from *Al-Kafi* illustrates the principle of *ghayb al-zawj* (husband's absence) in Shia jurisprudence, where a divorce executed by a third party on behalf of the fleeing husband is deemed valid. The Imam’s concise ruling, 'Marry, may Allah have mercy on you,' underscores the practical ease granted to women in such scenarios, avoiding the need for prolonged waiting periods (*iddah*) or complex judicial verification of the absent husband's intent. This case highlights the flexibility of Shia legal methodology in resolving marital status when the primary party is unreachable.
